text:
Áed, also written Aedh or Aodh, is an Irish hero and divinity. The name is common in ancient Irish legend. It was anglicized as Hugh. It gives rise to contemporary surnames including Hay, Hayes, Hughes, McHugh, and MacKay. Many legendary figures bear the name, each with his own story.

Áed Abrat was a fairy king. He was the father of the fairy queens Fand and Lí Ban. Little legend remains to define him.

Áed, son of Eochaid Lethderg of Leinster, was held captive by two fairy women for three years. Unlike most captives of fairy kidnapping, he sought to escape the beautiful but sterile land in which he was held. He succeeded. He then traveled to see Saint Patrick, who freed him from the lingering bonds of fairyland. The first part of the tale fits Irish mythology. The second part appears to have been added after the land was Christianized.

Áed, son of Lir, was one of the enchanted princes of the Children of Lir. His jealous stepmother turned him into a swan for nine hundred years.

Áed, king of Tara, was a sixth-century king. He owned a magical cow that he thought would keep him safe in battle. The belief may have been correct. Yet Áed left the cow at home when he went to war, and he was killed.

Áed Minbhrec, son of the Dagda, seduced the wife of the hero Coincheann. Coincheann killed Áed Minbhrec in retaliation. The Dagda condemned Coincheann to carry Áed's corpse until he found a boulder big enough to cover it. The story connects with Grianán Aileach, where Coincheann died of exhaustion from bearing boulder and body. Some variations have Áed alive and ruling from his fairy mound at Mullaghnasee, near Ballyshannon in County Donegal.

Áed, husband of Aíbell, a queen of Connacht, was deceived by the powerful king Mongán. Mongán shape-shifted into Áed's form to sleep with Aíbell. He put a transfigured crone into Áed's bed to cover the deception.

Áed Alain was the husband of the birth goddess Bébinn, sister of Bóand.

Áed Ruad was the father of the goddess and queen Macha Mong Rua. Macha ruled jointly with two other Ulster kings, Cimbáeth and Díthorba, in periods of seven years each. When Áed Ruad drowned in the waterfall Assaroe in County Donegal, Macha went to war for the right to succeed him. This Áed is considered an Otherworldly figure, sometimes identified with Goll Mac Morna, rather than a mere human king.

Áed, son of Miodhchaoin, was the killer of the Sons of Tuireann, the most tragic of Irish heroes. He was in turn killed by them.

Áed Eangach was the long-awaited king of Ireland. He was to be born miraculously from the side of a pillar on Tara. This red-handed king was never born. Yet the expectation of his imminent arrival was a staple of Irish poetic lore for centuries.

Áed Srónmár was the human lover of the goddess or fairy Ruad. He plays little part in myth. His role was to inspire his beloved's fatal trip from the Otherworld to join him on earth. Ruad died before reaching him.
objective: To record the many Irish heroes and divinities who bore the name Áed.
key_results: Áed was a common ancient Irish name anglicized as Hugh.
At least eleven distinct legendary figures bear the name.
Áed, son of Lir, was turned into a swan for 900 years.
Áed Ruad drowned at Assaroe; his daughter Macha went to war to succeed him.
Áed Eangach, the long-awaited king, was never born.
